title: Born at Talwandi, 1469
hookLine: Nanak is born to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta in a Punjab village now called Nankana Sahib
last: JAPJI SAHIB — 38 STANZAS, VERSE BY VERSE.

lines: A FAMILY, A VILLAGE, A BABY.
cards: Punjab, 1469, in the spring, if the oldest accounts are right. Wheat fields run flat to the horizon. A mud-brick village called Talwandi sits west of the city of Lahore.

The landlord is a Muslim named Rai Bular. His village accountant, who keeps the records of land and harvests, is a Hindu named Mehta Kalu. And in Kalu's house, his wife, Mata Tripta, is about to have her second child.
No palace, no crowd outside. Just a family, a village, a baby.

teach.b: The baby was Nanak. His father was a Khatri, from a caste of traders and record-keepers: a practical man who hoped his son would earn a respectable living.
His mother is remembered in Sikh tradition for her gentleness and her quiet faith in her unusual son. There was an older sister, Nanaki, and she gets her own day tomorrow.
The janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, surround the birth with signs: a room filled with light, a midwife who said she'd never seen a child like this. Sikhs tell those stories with joy.
What can be said plainly is where, and roughly when. And here's an honest wrinkle.
The oldest accounts put the birth in spring, in the month of Vaisakh. But Sikhs usually celebrate it at the full moon of Kartik, in October or November, following another early tradition.
Scholars still argue about the date. The celebration stays in autumn, with lights, processions and all-night singing, and nobody's faith hangs on the calendar.
As for the village: Talwandi is now called Nankana Sahib, Nanak's town, and since partition it has been in Pakistan.
A gurdwara stands where tradition says he was born, and Sikh pilgrims still cross the border to visit it. A boy born in a village with a Muslim landlord and a Hindu accountant.
It fits, somehow, for the man who'd say there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

how: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's birth each year, usually at the full moon of Kartik in the autumn, with processions, continuous readings of the scripture, kirtan and langar; many make pilgrimage to Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.

practice: Sit comfortably and say, quietly, the name of the place where your life began: a town, a hospital, a house. If you don't know much about it, picture what you imagine.
Then name the people who were there, or waiting, as far as you know them. Nobody there knew what your life would be. Notice how small and ordinary that beginning was, and how much has grown from it.
